title: FromSoftware's Soulsborne Games Ranked From Easiest to Hardest
description: From the freedom of Elden Ring to the precision demanded by Sekiro, we rank seven landmark FromSoftware adventures by the difficulty of a normal first playthrough.
body:
Difficulty in a FromSoftware game is never just about enemy damage. Level design, boss speed, healing systems, build freedom, checkpoints, and the amount of help available all shape how demanding a first playthrough feels.

This ranking considers each base game in its standard form. It assumes a blind or lightly guided first run, allows the tools each game naturally provides, and does not factor in challenge runs, downloadable expansions, or deliberately overpowered late-game builds. Individual experience will still vary—and that is part of what makes this debate fun.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: FromSoftware's Soulsborne Games Ranked From Easiest to Hardest

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring contains some of FromSoftware’s most demanding individual encounters, but its open structure gives players more control over when and how they face them. If a boss feels overwhelming, the Lands Between almost always offers another cave, quest, weapon, upgrade, or region to explore first.

Spirit Ashes, multiplayer summons, powerful status effects, and an enormous range of builds create multiple answers to the same obstacle. That accessibility does not make the game easy; it makes difficulty more adjustable than in the studio’s earlier, more linear adventures.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring lets players leave a difficult encounter and return with a stronger build.
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished overlooking the vast landscape of the Lands Between.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The most flexible path through the formula
contentBlocks.platforms: PC, PS4, PS5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S

contentBlocks.text:
Demon’s Souls is mechanically slower and more limited than the games that followed it. Many bosses are built around a readable trick or environmental idea, so discovering the intended solution can matter more than mastering a long sequence of reactions.

The real pressure comes from the journey. Long runs back to bosses, scarce healing early on, World Tendency, and levels filled with traps can punish carelessness severely. Once its systems are understood, however, its combat challenges are generally more manageable than those of later FromSoftware games.
contentBlocks.caption: Demon’s Souls often places its harshest challenge between the player and the boss arena.
contentBlocks.heading: Demon's Souls
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A lone warrior exploring the ruined kingdom of Boletaria.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Simpler combat wrapped in unforgiving level design

contentBlocks.text:
Dark Souls rewards caution more than raw speed. Shields are extremely effective, enemies usually telegraph their attacks clearly, and a careful player can control most encounters one opponent at a time. Its connected world also allows knowledge to become a powerful advantage on later attempts.

What makes the first journey difficult is uncertainty. Important mechanics are barely explained, routes can lead into areas meant for later, and a poor choice of equipment can make progress feel much harder. The game becomes dramatically easier once the player learns how its world fits together.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls is demanding at first, but knowledge steadily turns Lordran into familiar territory.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls Remastered
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Chosen Undead crossing one of Lordran’s interconnected environments.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A deliberate test of patience and observation
contentBlocks.platforms: PC, PS4, Xbox One, Nintendo Switch

contentBlocks.text:
Dark Souls II is not always the fastest game in the series, but it constantly tests positioning and resource management. Groups of enemies, long combat spaces, limited early healing, weapon durability, and the Adaptability stat can make the opening hours especially uncomfortable.

Scholar of the First Sin also rearranges encounters and frequently places pressure on players from several directions. Its enormous build variety eventually provides strong solutions, but reaching that point requires learning a slightly different rhythm from the rest of the trilogy.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls II frequently increases difficulty through enemy placement and sustained pressure.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Bearer of the Curse facing multiple threats in the kingdom of Drangleic.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Attrition, ambushes, and the danger of being surrounded

contentBlocks.text:
Dark Souls III keeps the familiar stamina-based foundation but dramatically raises the speed of its major encounters. Bosses chain attacks together, delay their timing, transform between phases, and punish healing attempts more aggressively than in the earlier Dark Souls games.

The game is more linear and its controls are highly responsive, which reduces some confusion outside combat. Even so, the late-game boss roster demands reliable dodging, careful stamina use, and the ability to adapt when a familiar pattern suddenly changes.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls III combines clear controls with some of the trilogy’s fastest and most complex bosses.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls III
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Ashen One confronting one of Lothric’s towering enemies.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Faster bosses leave less room to breathe

contentBlocks.text:
Bloodborne removes the comfort of a strong shield and asks players to fight at close range. The regain system can restore recently lost health through immediate counterattacks, while firearms reward precise parries. Both mechanics push the player toward danger instead of allowing them to wait safely.

Its opening area is a severe introduction, healing items must be replenished, and several bosses combine speed with unpredictable movement. Players who adapt to its aggressive rhythm may eventually find it liberating, but the transition from defensive Souls habits can be brutal.
contentBlocks.caption: Bloodborne turns forward pressure and quick reactions into essential defensive tools.
contentBlocks.heading: Bloodborne
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Hunter moving through the gothic streets of Yharnam.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Aggression is not optional—it is the survival system

contentBlocks.text:
Sekiro is the hardest FromSoftware game on this list because it offers fewer ways to avoid learning its central skill. Character builds, summoned allies, and traditional level grinding cannot replace the need to deflect attacks, manage posture, read perilous moves, and control the pace of a duel.

The result is a steep but unusually honest learning curve. Major opponents act like examinations of mechanics introduced throughout the game, and progress often depends on changing the player’s habits rather than improving a statistic. Once its rhythm clicks, Sekiro can feel remarkably precise—but earning that confidence is the toughest first-playthrough challenge FromSoftware has created.
contentBlocks.caption: Sekiro’s hardest encounters demand mastery of deflection, posture, and attack recognition.
contentBlocks.heading: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The shinobi Wolf in a fierce sword duel.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A focused combat system that demands true mastery

quickRead: The most flexible path through the formula
Simpler combat wrapped in unforgiving level design
A deliberate test of patience and observation
conclusion:
==No FromSoftware difficulty ranking can be universal. A player who thrives on aggressive combat may find Bloodborne more forgiving than Dark Souls, while someone who enjoys exploration and build crafting may have a smoother journey through Elden Ring.
==
==What makes these games memorable is not simply how often they defeat the player, but how clearly they teach persistence, observation, and adaptation. Sekiro earns the hardest position here because it demands the narrowest form of mastery—but the most difficult FromSoftware game will always be the one whose lessons challenge your natural playstyle.==
